How to look at an image
A repeatable way to see what an image is actually doing, instead of only noticing whether you like it.
8 min

Shape, texture and pattern
Three of the basic elements every image is made of, and the fact that connects them — they are the same thing seen from three distances.
10 min

Contrast
Difference — how much a part of a picture differs from what sits next to it. An edge exists only where something changes, so contrast is what makes anything visible at all.
8 min

Visual hierarchy
The order in which your eye visits the parts of an image — decided by the image, not by you.
9 min

Balance
Why one frame feels steady on its feet and another feels like it is tipping over, even though nothing in a picture weighs anything.
8 min

Negative space
The empty parts of an image are shapes too, and you are composing them whether you notice or not.
8 min

The rule of thirds
A beginner's grid that mostly earns its keep by stopping you putting everything dead centre — genuinely useful, and far weaker than its reputation.
8 min

Framing and cropping
The frame is a decision about what is in the picture and what is not. The crop is the cheapest powerful edit there is — which also makes it the easiest way to throw the subject away.
9 min

Edges and merges
Where two areas meet, and what happens when they meet badly. An edge you cannot find is a tool when it was intended and a defect when it was not.
9 min

Lines and movement
A line in a picture is hardly ever drawn. It is an edge, an alignment, a gaze or a trajectory — and its job is to give the eye a direction to travel in and a speed to travel at.
9 min

Rhythm and repetition
Repeating something turns many things into one thing — and the moment it does, whatever does not belong to the set becomes impossible to miss.
9 min

Scale and proportion
Scale is how big something looks compared with something you already know. Proportion is how the parts of one thing relate to each other. They share a word and almost nothing else.
9 min

Simplification
Every element you add divides the viewer's attention, so the question about anything in the frame is never whether it is nice but what it is doing. Taking things out is the hardest edit there is.
8 min

Depth cues
A picture is a flat surface. It reads as deep because a dozen separate cues all point the same way, and your eye believes the majority.
7 min

Linear perspective
Parallel lines in the world meet at a point in the picture, because equal real distances take up less of your view the further away they are.
8 min

Atmospheric perspective
Distant things go pale, flat and sky-coloured because you are looking at them through more air, and air scatters light.
8 min

Light direction
Where the light sits relative to the subject and to the camera. It decides where the shadows land and how much of the shaded side you get to see, which is what makes a flat picture look solid.
9 min

Hard and soft light
Whether shadows have crisp edges or fade gradually. It is decided by one thing — how big the light looks from where the subject is standing.
8 min

Light falloff
How fast light gets dimmer as it travels away from its source. The useful part is that it changes fastest right next to the lamp and barely at all far away.
9 min

The anatomy of a shadow
The named parts of light and shade on a solid object — highlight, halftone, core shadow, reflected light, cast shadow, contact shadow — and the rules each one obeys.
9 min

Value structure
How light or dark things are, independent of their colour. Squint at any image and what survives is its value structure — and if that does not read, no colour will save it.
9 min

Hue, value and chroma
A colour is not one thing. It is three independent dials — which colour it is, how light it is, and how far it sits from grey — and most arguments about colour are two people turning different dials.
7 min

The colour wheel, and why there is more than one
A ring of hues in spectral order, closed at the join by colours no wavelength can make. It is a working model, not a picture of light — and different jobs need different wheels, which is why they disagree about what sits opposite what.
8 min

The colour of the light
What you see is the object's own colour multiplied by the light's colour — and your brain quietly divides the light back out, which is why a white shirt looks white everywhere.
8 min

Complementary colours
The pair of colours that cancel each other. There are two different pairs answering to that name — the one that mixes to grey and the one your eye pairs — and they are almost never the same colour.
10 min

How to choose colours
A practical order of operations for picking colours — decide the job, choose on all three dials, then set the areas — and an honest account of why the named schemes explain much less than they claim.
10 min

Diffuse and specular
Light hitting a surface either goes in and comes back out coloured, or bounces straight off keeping the light's own colour. Almost everything a material looks like follows from the split between those two.
9 min

Metal and everything else
Metals have almost no colour of their own and show you the room instead; everything else gets its colour from underneath and reflects the light's own colour on top. This is the sharpest material test you can run on an image.
10 min

Roughness and Fresnel
Two dials that finish a material. Roughness decides how blurry the reflection is; Fresnel makes every surface more reflective at glancing angles. Between them they explain why real objects are never evenly shiny.
10 min

Focal length vs camera position
Where the camera stands decides how big near things look next to far things. The lens only decides how much of that view fits in the frame.
7 min

Depth of field
The band of distance that comes out looking sharp. Everything outside it blurs, and how that blur grows tells you whether a picture came out of a real camera.
7 min

Exposure and dynamic range
How much light got recorded, and how far apart the brightest and darkest thing can be before one of them stops recording at all.
8 min

Gestalt grouping
The automatic machinery that turns a field of pixels into objects and groups — and the reason accidental alignments in a photograph look deliberate.
8 min

Naming what is wrong
A checklist for turning "something looks off" into a specific, defensible sentence about the image.
9 min

The stock look
What the stock genre looks like, and the two directions a generated image slides into it - generic ornament piled onto a logo, and texture smeared and drained out of a surface. Measured, with our own pairs.
9 min

What a logo does
A mark has one job — to identify one thing and tell it apart from everything else. It does not explain the business and it cannot make the business good; the meaning runs the other way.
7 min

Identity systems
The set of decisions that make a mark work everywhere — colour, typeface, grid, formats, signage, artwork masters and the rules about who may change what. Its real purpose is governance, not beauty.
8 min

Logo reproduction tests
The set of physical conditions a mark has to survive — one colour, small size, reversed on dark, blurred, stitched, next to competitors — and the mechanism that makes each one fail.
8 min

Type anatomy
The named parts of a letter, and which of them actually decide whether a page is easy to read rather than merely pretty.
7 min

Legibility and readability
Two different measurements that get treated as one — whether you can tell the characters apart, and whether you can get through a paragraph without effort.
7 min

Measure and line height
The two settings that decide whether body text is comfortable — how long the lines are, and how far apart. They have to be chosen together.
8 min

Beyond Latin
Most typographic advice is advice about Latin. This is which parts of it come from the eye, which parts are Latin-only conventions, and what other writing systems do instead.
8 min

Poster mechanisms
The named moves a poster can make on a passer-by — fourteen of them, several arranged as deliberate opposites — and why they are moves rather than styles.
8 min

The first read
What is left of a poster when you are far away and not paying attention — and the five or six tests that tell you whether that residue still carries the message.
8 min

Grids
A set of decisions taken once — margins, columns, gutters, modules, baselines — so that no later page needs a fresh decision. It is a system, not a look.
8 min

Type hierarchy on a page
How a reader finds their way through a page without being told — by size, weight, space, position and case. Space does more of the work than size does.
8 min

How accurately a chart can be read
The property of the ink that carries a number — position, length, angle, area, shading — decides how wrong the reader will be. The order is not a matter of taste; it was measured.
7 min

Choosing a chart
Start from the relationship in the data and the question in the reader's head. The chart type is the last decision you make, not the first.
7 min

When a chart lies
The dangerous chart is not the ugly one. It is the one where every number is correct and the picture still argues for something the numbers do not support.
7 min

Icon, pictogram, symbol, glyph, logo
Five words the field uses interchangeably for five different things. Knowing which one you are looking at tells you what test it has to pass.
6 min

Testing whether a symbol works
You cannot tell whether a symbol is understood by looking at it, because you already know the answer. You find out by testing strangers — and the results are boringly repeatable.
7 min

Wayfinding is not signage
Signage is the objects on the wall. Wayfinding is a stranger actually arriving. You can add signs and make wayfinding worse.
8 min

Sign legibility is arithmetic
How big, how thick, how far apart, how much contrast. Most of it is calculated from viewing distance and mounting height, and the legal numbers are floors rather than goals.
8 min

Packaging hierarchy
Ordering what a pack says, under constraints no other graphic design job has — a reader who is standing up, holding it, deciding in seconds, from a metre away, next to fifty rivals, with part of the layout dictated by law.
8 min

Packaging you can actually open
The point where packaging graphics meet hands and eyes — opening force, tactile cues, contrast on a curved glossy surface, and the barcode rules designers usually meet only after the print run.
8 min

Motion as information
Movement used to tell the reader something — where a thing came from, and that it is still the same thing. Motion is the loudest signal an interface has, which is why spending it on decoration is expensive.
8 min

Timing and restraint
How long an interface animation should last, which curve it should follow, and why every one of them has to be switchable off. The usable window is roughly 100 to 500 milliseconds.
8 min

Design tokens
A named decision. The point of calling a colour color.text.default rather than #1B1B1B is that the name can be pointed somewhere else once, for everybody.
7 min

Type scales and spacing scales
The two most-used scales in any design system — a short list of text sizes and a short list of gaps. Both work only if adjacent steps are far enough apart to look deliberate.
8 min

Colour management
Why a colour on your screen is not a colour on paper, and the machinery — gamuts, profiles, a shared connection space and four rendering intents — that decides which compromise you get.
9 min

Print-ready files
What survives the trip to a press — PDF/X as a deliberately restricted subset of PDF, bleed and trim as consequences of a blade, and why "is this print-ready" is answered by the printer's spec sheet rather than by a file format.
8 min

Raster and vector
Two ways of storing a picture — a grid of samples, or the geometry of the shapes. Which one a file uses decides what you may safely do to it.
8 min

Paths and curves
What a vector shape is made of — anchors, control points, segments — and why the same outline drawn with twenty anchors is better than the same outline traced with four hundred.
6 min

What an SVG actually contains
SVG is an XML document that may hold geometry, live text, an embedded photograph, links to other servers, filters and scripts. So the extension proves nothing — and the file is readable text, which is how you check.
7 min

AI, EPS and PDF
Three containers people call "vector formats". What each really holds, what survives being opened somewhere else, and what outlining the text destroys on the way.
6 min

What a bad vector file looks like
The faults you can see — hairlines that vanish, spikes on sharp corners, banded gradients, artwork hidden rather than removed, tiled seams, substituted fonts and traced mush — and the size to look at each one.
8 min

How images mean
The gap between what an image shows and what a viewer takes it to mean — and the four things that gap is made of: signs, connotation, codes and modality.
8 min

The ethics of making and choosing images
An image can be true in every detail and still argue for something false. What that means for the person choosing the image, and for the people in it.
8 min

What a map decides
Everything on a map matters to somebody and it all has to fit in one plane. Five principles decide what wins — and the first real decision is which question the map is for.
9 min

Map furniture and map colour
The standard parts of a map and what each is actually for, then how to pick a colour scheme from the shape of the data — and why a rainbow ruins ordered data.
9 min
